worst_places.quote: The double-checked locking issue in this code allows race conditions where two threads both see instance == null, both create instances, and overwrite each other. This defeats the Singleton guarantee. Options B, C, and D are either false or not primary pitfalls of Singletons in concurrent code.
worst_places.problem: oop-patterns-quiz-11 (and identically quiz-16, quiz-21). The explanation names the fix as if it were the bug: the code shown has no locking at all — plain lazy `if (instance == null)`. Double-checked locking is the standard *remedy*, so a reader who trusts the explanation learns the term backwards. Compounding it, the explanation refers to 'Options B, C, and D' while the UI renders four unlettered options, so the target reader has to guess whether 'B' means the second option or the second wrong one. And the whole item tests JVM thread safety in a site whose articles are 100% TypeScript/Node — content/topics/oop-patterns/ru/03-creational-patterns.md lists Singleton's three problems as hidden dependency, global mutable state and SRP violation, and never mentions threads, because JS has no shared-memory threads.
worst_places.before: The double-checked locking issue in this code allows race conditions where two threads both see instance == null, both create instances, and overwrite each other. This defeats the Singleton guarantee. Options B, C, and D are either false or not primary pitfalls of Singletons in concurrent code.
worst_places.after: This lazy `getInstance()` has no synchronisation at all. Two threads can both reach the `instance == null` check before either has assigned, so both build an instance and one overwrites the other — the Singleton guarantee is gone. The usual fix is double-checked locking: a `volatile` field plus a `synchronized` block around the second null check. Note this is a JVM problem. In Node.js there is one thread per process, so the Node equivalent of this bug is not a race — it is the module cache handing every test file the same mutable instance (see the Singleton article).

worst_places.quote: HOC is JavaScript's implementation of Decorator; the key difference is that HOC wraps components at runtime while Decorator wraps classes at definition time
worst_places.problem: This is the correct option of oop-patterns-quiz-5. Twelve items later, the correct option of oop-patterns-quiz-10 in the same file says the opposite: 'Decorator modifies object instances at runtime; HOC creates wrapper components that compose React components'. Both cannot be right. The articles side with quiz-10: content/topics/oop-patterns/ru/04-structural-patterns.md defines Decorator as «Динамически добавляет объекту новые обязанности» and explicitly separates the GoF pattern from TypeScript `@Decorator` annotations — «это Decorator паттерн по духу, но не по классической GoF-структуре». So quiz-5 teaches the annotation as if it were the GoF pattern, contradicting both the article and its own sibling quiz item.
worst_places.before: HOC is JavaScript's implementation of Decorator; the key difference is that HOC wraps components at runtime while Decorator wraps classes at definition time
worst_places.after: HOC is React's functional form of Decorator; both wrap at runtime, but a classic Decorator wraps an object instance while an HOC wraps a component and returns a new one

worst_places.quote: The classical decorator's core guarantee — every layer implements the *exact same* interface as what it wraps — doesn't fully hold for HOCs. `withAuth` and `withLogging` both need to decide what props to pass down, and if two HOCs each inject their own prop under the same key (say, both add a `data` prop from different sources), the innermost HOC's assignment silently wins or loses depending on spread order — there's no compile-time guarantee of prop-name collision the way there would be with a strictly typed interface method.

Nothing warns you at compile time, because there is no shared interface here to check the names against — a strictly typed interface method would have caught it.

patterns: THE TEMPLATE MECHANISM HOLDS, AND IT IS NOW A SITE-WIDE RULE. The article template has a bullet slot, a ```txt diagram slot and an ❌/✅ code-pair slot; the bank template has none of the three. Counted across the 8 RU articles: 119 markdown bullets, 39 ```txt diagrams, 81 ❌/✅ markers. Counted across the 34 RU bank answers: 3 bullets (all in one answer), 0 diagrams, 0 ❌/✅ pairs. Every bank answer is the same fixed shape — `### heading` / one-sentence definition / one code fence / one or two undifferentiated prose paragraphs / `**Частая ловушка:**`. With no slot to put a list in, every enumeration collapses into a single sentence. That is the whole 26.2-vs-11.2 gap: long-sentence rate is 0-2% in the RU articles and 42.9% in the RU bank; 3.5-13.1% in the EN articles and 61.3% in the EN bank. The connector differs from `architecture` — there the collapsed list was a semicolon chain, here it is an em-dash + comma + parenthetical chain (prose semicolons are only 2.7x denser in the bank, 4.3 vs 1.6 per 1k, while em-dashes are actually *less* dense than in the articles) — but the cause is identical and the fix is identical: give the bank template a bullet slot and a diagram slot. The clinching evidence is internal: oop-patterns-q-5 is the single answer in the file that uses a bulleted list (the three cloning approaches), and it is by a wide margin the clearest answer in the bank, written by the same author on the same day.

THE QUIZ IS FIVE QUESTIONS ASKED FIVE TIMES EACH, AND IT TESTS A DIFFERENT LANGUAGE THAN THE ARTICLES. The 25 items cover six distinct ideas: Singleton thread-safety (items 1, 6, 11, 16, 21 — five near-verbatim restatements, three of them with the same Java `getInstance()` snippet), Factory vs Abstract Factory (7, 12, 17, 22), Observer vs Pub/Sub (3, 13, 18, 23), Strategy vs State (4, 9, 14, 19, 24), HOC vs Decorator (5, 10, 15, 20, 25), plus items 2 and 8. Zero items on SOLID, zero on GRASP, zero on Builder, Prototype, Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy, Command, Iterator, Template Method, Mediator or Chain of Responsibility — i.e. six of the eight articles are untested. Worse, the six Singleton items test JVM shared-memory threading (`synchronized`, `volatile`, reflection and deserialisation attacks, JVM class loading), which the articles never mention and cannot mention: content/topics/oop-patterns/ru/03-creational-patterns.md frames Singleton's three problems as hidden dependency, global mutable state and SRP violation, and content/questions/oop-patterns.json q-8 says «Синглтоны в Node.js — это синглтоны на уровне модуля». A reader who studies the articles will not have been taught anything the Singleton quiz items ask.

THE BANK'S FIRST SENTENCES ARE THE ZONE'S ONE UNQUALIFIED SUCCESS — AND THE MODEL FOR EVERYTHING ELSE. Rubric C is the bank's best score (4/5, and 0.0% indirect leads mechanically). All 34 answers open with a plain-language one-sentence definition that answers the question asked before any caveat arrives: «Multiton — это Singleton, обобщённый на фиксированный набор именованных инстансов вместо ровно одного», «Facade предоставляет единый упрощённый интерфейс поверх набора подсистем». The failure is that the discipline stops after sentence one. Sentence two routinely runs 60-86 words and stacks three or four new ideas. The style-guide rule to extract: apply the first-sentence discipline to the *second and third* paragraph leads too — every paragraph of a bank answer should open with its own short claim, then support it, rather than opening mid-argument with 'The cost interview answers usually skip:' followed by 62 words.
